doc.title: Ada Rovatti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 13, 2022

title: Jazz as art in Europe and not America's classical music
summary: Europe valued jazz as art early, tied to racism in the US; both agree to just call it jazz.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And it’s interesting and a bit ironic that jazz was thought of as an art form first in Europe, not here. People did scholarly writing about it and all that kind of thing.

Yeah it was more appreciated. Also it has to do also with racism here in this country and in Europe. Just the way also I remember I grew up I was always kind of interested about when a musician would come and tour in Italy it was like a black musician it was like kind of cool. It was like there was not — you add something even more exotic and more interesting. So I think that they didn’t have to deal with the racism that there was here. And it just really is an art form. I think that’s when Europe got it right right away. It was an art form. Here it took a little longer to be fully appreciated.
Yes. But at the same time as you mentioned earlier, it behooves it to have an entertainment aspect to it also. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Otherwise, sometimes you hear, there’s a phrase that has gone around like jazz is America’s classical music. And some people — no we don’t need it to be America’s classical music. Just let it be jazz.

Yeah no that’s true. Because there is American classical music. They are two different things. There are plenty of classical. I mean I do understand like when they try to mean it like in saying that it’s just like the root word. We, in Europe there’s classical music here, the American classical music, but no. Just let it be jazz.
